hits.name: swyx
hits.hook: swyx: Dots is the DevDay 'one more thing'; always-on agents have been in the works longer than the launch narrative.
hits.draft_en:
swyx's "one more thing" note on Dots is the distribution reminder: OpenAI had been shipping toward always-on agents before the keynote slide.

The quote is OpenAI's Dots launch (GPT-6 Astra, always-on agents). Builder takeaway is not the merch energy. It is that proactive agents change the failure mode from "bad answer" to "bad interruption." Spend caps, allowlists, and quiet hours matter more than another demo reel.

If you are building Dots-class loops, instrument when the agent spoke first and whether the user acted or muted. That metric beats vanity task-complete rates.

hits.name: Hamel Husain
hits.hook: Hamel: stop the 'keep the laptop open' insanity; SSH or remote Codex onto a Mac mini once you have been burned three times.
hits.draft_en:
Hamel dunking on the keep-laptop-open workflow is correct and overdue.

Once an agent run needs hours, a sleeping lid is an outage. SSH, a mini that stays awake, or a real remote runtime is the fix. Same lesson as durable runtimes: if the loop dies when you close the laptop, you do not have a harness.

Checklist: headless host, wake lock or always-on box, resume after disconnect, and a stuck-run owner. Laptop-as-server is a demo habit.

hits.name: Ethan Mollick
hits.hook: Mollick uploads the Bitter Lesson music video to YouTube after the Dot/swarm essay on agents self-organizing.
hits.draft_en:
Ethan posting the Bitter Lesson video to YouTube is distribution hygiene for a thesis he already wrote: self-organizing task progress is what he underestimated, and it shows up in Muse/Dots-class agents.

Useful for builders as a shareable explainer, not as a new claim. Pair it with a concrete harness metric: how often does your agent replan without a human prompt, and how often is that replanning waste.

If you quote this, add one number from your own runs. The video is the hook; your log is the substance.

hits.hook: Mollick: 'we're so early' is self-congratulation; senior leaders already get AI, company change is the slow part.
hits.draft_en:
Ethan's pushback on 'we're so early' matches what I see in operator work.

Plenty of execs are vibecoding, adopting Claude, and finding workflows. The lag is org change: permissions, eval ownership, and who is accountable when an agent spends money. Timeline swagger does not rewrite those constraints.

If your pitch needs 'everyone is asleep,' update it. Sell change management and runtime controls, not early-adopter cosplay.

Hamel's evals interview lesson is the hiring signal under the launch noise.

Evals showing up in job posts means companies want people who can design traps, structure take-homes, and read failure modes, not people who only recite model cards. If you are hiring agent builders, ask for a binary failure taxonomy and a labeling plan, not a vibes deck.

hits.name: Ethan Mollick
hits.hook: Mollick quotes the narrow claim: AI may already hit junior white-collar hiring margins; aggregate disruption not in the data yet.
hits.draft_en:
Ethan's share of the 'narrow claim' labor note is the disciplined version of the doom chart.

Maybe AI already bends hiring at the junior margin for exposed roles. Aggregate disruption is still contested and not clean in the data. That split matters for agent builders: automate well-defined junior tasks, redesign the role around review and exceptions, and do not pretend macro employment has already flipped.

Measure your own hiring funnel and task rubric before you cite anyone else's Substack.
hits.video_tip: Talking-head 25s: Margin effects != macro collapse. Caption: Local rubric before headcount slides.

Remembering people, roles, and preferences across runs is where demos die in enterprises: permissions, stale facts, and silent wrong memories. If Managed Deep Agents 0.8 improves person-memory, the test is wrong-memory rate under real ACL boundaries, not a launch GIF.

hits.name: Jerry Liu
hits.hook: Jerry: Extract v2.5 hits 93-96%+ on dense long-list table extraction where Astra sits ~30%; every value attributed to source.
hits.draft_en:
Jerry's dense-table Extract numbers are the specialist-agent case again.

Long lists and cross-page cells are where frontier VLMs stop early or lose attribution. Claiming 93-96%+ vs ~30% Astra on that slice is a strong hypothesis. Treat it as one until you rerun on your messiest multi-page insurance or filing PDFs.

If extraction is core, grounded citations plus layout-aware agents usually beat another general VLM pass. Re-bench before you swap.
hits.video_tip: Flash table extraction clip 8s if available, then notepad: Re-run on YOUR worst PDFs. Caption: Specialist + citations > generalist stops. Warn: launch video not fully reviewed here.
hits.text:
one of the most challenging tasks for frontier models is being able to extract thousands of values from extremely dense tables in documents.

our new Extract v2.5 agents are able to get 93%-96%+ on long-list extraction, including cells that fall in between pages. 

in contrast, astra gets ~30% accuracy over this benchmark. 

in these cases, frontier VLMs can stop early or miss repeated records. 

they also struggle to attribute each value back to the source. we are able to attribute every single extracted value back to the source.

check out the video below, the blog post, and llamaparse!

hits.name: Harrison Chase
hits.hook: Harrison: Google multi-agent proof paper; verifier starts from clean context so the explorer cannot talk it into a bad proof.
hits.draft_en:
Harrison pulling the clean-context verifier pattern from the Google proof-discovery paper is load-bearing for agent harnesses.

Explorer gets freedom to try wild ideas. Verifier starts fresh so it cannot be talked into a bad proof. Same reason Deep Agents subagents get their own context. Shared polluted context is how agents launder mistakes.

Design rule: generation context and judgment context stay separate. If your judge reads the chain-of-thought that sold the answer, you built a rubber stamp.

virals.name: elvis
virals.hook: Google Research multi-agent proof discovery; clean-context verifier pattern (~21k views).
virals.text:
Banger paper from Google Research on multi-agent proof discovery.

(bookmark it)

It's really interesting to see this emerging multi-agent pattern: not enforcing too much execution structure and pairing it with dedicated agents for advising and verification.

I think it is generally applicable as well. Great read.

Here is how it works:

Cogentic runs on Gemini and works on open problems in theoretical computer science, starting from the problem statement with no expert hints.

The system works in rounds, and the orchestrator decides how many provers to run in each round. Every prover gets one direction to work on, such as a specific bound or a counterexample search, plus a short briefing that a summarizer agent writes from earlier attempts and verifier feedback. Each summarizer writes its briefing independently, so provers in the same round read different summaries of the same history.

Each draft goes through two adversarial verifiers. One checks the draft on its own, and the other reads all of the round's drafts side by side to catch shared mistakes. A draft is accepted only if both pass it.

The agents share state through two disk documents. A record logs every attempt with the objection it failed on, and a ledger stores verified lemmas and ruled-out directions. An auditor extracts correct lemmas from rejected proofs, verifies them again independently, and adds them to the ledger.

A separate process advisor reads the verification logs across rounds and updates the instructions given to provers and verifiers. The orchestrator and the advisor can't give mathematical opinions, so the provers provide all the math.

It produced new results on five open problems in online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design, each checked by domain experts. Most problems took around 100 Gemini calls, and the hardest took around 1,000.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40324

Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/cogentic-multi-agent-orchestration-for-automated-proof-discovery-2609.40324

Today we’re introducing Extract v2.5 - a series of frontier agents tuned for document extraction.

The agents (cost-effective, agentic, agentic plus) are tuned for value accuracy and grounding. Our extraction agents outperform Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol while being 30%-4x cheaper. 

We’ve made massive improvements on complex extraction over 
* long lists (86.1% -> 95.5% on our agentic tier)
* records spanning pages (85.5% -> 96.5%)
* scanned forms (90.9% -> 95.7%)

✅ Structural Reasoning: we tailor document extraction algorithms depending on the type, layout, and information

Our extraction agents are SOTA in price-performance on ExtractBench, across a wide range of cost points. We are the best tool for document extraction across documents of any complexity.

Blog: https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-extract-v2-5

outsiders.name: elvis
outsiders.hook: Google Research multi-agent proof discovery; clean-context verifier pattern (~21k views).
outsiders.text:
Banger paper from Google Research on multi-agent proof discovery.

(bookmark it)

It's really interesting to see this emerging multi-agent pattern: not enforcing too much execution structure and pairing it with dedicated agents for advising and verification.

I think it is generally applicable as well. Great read.

Here is how it works:

Cogentic runs on Gemini and works on open problems in theoretical computer science, starting from the problem statement with no expert hints.

The system works in rounds, and the orchestrator decides how many provers to run in each round. Every prover gets one direction to work on, such as a specific bound or a counterexample search, plus a short briefing that a summarizer agent writes from earlier attempts and verifier feedback. Each summarizer writes its briefing independently, so provers in the same round read different summaries of the same history.

Each draft goes through two adversarial verifiers. One checks the draft on its own, and the other reads all of the round's drafts side by side to catch shared mistakes. A draft is accepted only if both pass it.

The agents share state through two disk documents. A record logs every attempt with the objection it failed on, and a ledger stores verified lemmas and ruled-out directions. An auditor extracts correct lemmas from rejected proofs, verifies them again independently, and adds them to the ledger.

A separate process advisor reads the verification logs across rounds and updates the instructions given to provers and verifiers. The orchestrator and the advisor can't give mathematical opinions, so the provers provide all the math.

It produced new results on five open problems in online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design, each checked by domain experts. Most problems took around 100 Gemini calls, and the hardest took around 1,000.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40324

Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/cogentic-multi-agent-orchestration-for-automated-proof-discovery-2609.40324
